findings.lesson_text: He compares himself to the mythological hunter Actaeon, turned into a stag by his own desires: 'O, when mine eyes did see Olivia first … That instant was I turned into a hart, / And my desires, like fell and cruel hounds, / E'er since pursue me'. The Actaeon allusion is telling: just as Actaeon was destroyed by his own hunting dogs, Orsino is consumed by his own desires.
findings.issue: The lesson states Actaeon was 'turned into a stag by his own desires'. In the myth, Actaeon was transformed into a stag by the goddess Diana (Artemis) as punishment for accidentally seeing her bathing — he did not transform himself. The lesson correctly identifies that his hunting hounds destroyed him, but misattributes the cause of the transformation to his desires rather than to Diana's curse. This is a factual error about the classical source.
findings.canonical_truth: In the myth (Ovid's Metamorphoses), Actaeon stumbled upon Diana bathing naked in a spring. Outraged, Diana splashed water on him, transforming him into a stag as punishment. His own hunting dogs then tore him apart, failing to recognise their master. Actaeon did not transform through desire; he was punished by Diana for an act of inadvertent transgression. Shakespeare uses the myth in Act 1, Scene 1 to show how Orsino, like Actaeon, is destroyed by forces set in motion the moment he saw his quarry — but the transformation agent is the goddess, not the hunter's own will.

findings.lesson_text: In Act 4, Scene 2, he admits: 'I would we were well rid of this knavery. If he may be conveniently delivered, I am now so far in offence with my niece that I cannot pursue with any safety this sport to the like conclusion.'
findings.issue: The lesson misquotes the final phrase of Sir Toby's speech. The actual text ends 'this sport to the upshot', not 'to the like conclusion'. 'Upshot' means the final outcome — a very specific Elizabethan term meaning the final shot or conclusive result. 'Like conclusion' is not in the text and changes the register and meaning of the phrase. Students who copy this quotation for the exam will be citing an inaccurate version.
findings.canonical_truth: Sir Toby's exact line (Act 4, Scene 2): 'I would we were well rid of this knavery. If he may be conveniently delivered, I would he were, for I am now so far in offence with my niece that I cannot pursue with any safety this sport to the upshot.' Note also that the lesson omits the intervening clause 'I would he were' present in the original.

findings.lesson_text: She lifts her veil ('Tis in grain, sir; 'twill endure wind and weather', 1.5), revealing her face and symbolically opening herself to the world again.
findings.issue: The lesson implies that the line ''Tis in grain, sir; 'twill endure wind and weather' is what Olivia says when she lifts her veil, as if this line accompanies or describes the unveiling. In fact, Olivia lifts her veil at an earlier moment: 'we will draw the curtain and show you the picture' — at which point the stage direction reads 'Unveiling'. The line ''Tis in grain, sir' is her response to Cesario's subsequent compliment on her beauty ('Excellently done, if God did all'). The line is not spoken at the moment of lifting — it is spoken after the veil is already removed, as a comment on the naturalness of her colouring. Students learning this as the 'veil-lifting quotation' will misplace it in exam responses.
findings.canonical_truth: In Act 1, Scene 5, Olivia unveils herself after saying 'we will draw the curtain and show you the picture. Look you, sir, such a one I was this present' (stage direction: Unveiling). Cesario then compliments her ('Excellently done, if God did all'), and Olivia replies ''Tis in grain, sir; 'twill endure wind and weather' — meaning her beauty is natural and permanent. The unveiling line and the ''Tis in grain' line are two distinct moments separated by Cesario's compliment.

findings.lesson_text: His name literally means 'ill will' (from the Italian mal + volio)
findings.issue: The etymology is approximately correct but the breakdown 'mal + volio' is imprecise. The name derives from Italian 'mal' (bad/evil) and 'voglio', the first-person singular of 'volere' (to want/will). 'Volio' is not an Italian word; 'voglio' is. The lesson's transcription omits the 'g' of 'voglio', which could confuse students attempting to apply or recall the etymology. The meaning 'ill will' is correct.
findings.canonical_truth: Malvolio derives from Italian 'male' (bad) + 'voglio' (I want / I will — first person singular of 'volere', to want or to will). The compound gives 'mal-voglio' = ill will / bad wish. The name was invented by Shakespeare as a character-defining signifier. See Behind the Name and the Malvolio Wikipedia article.

findings.lesson_text: His opening line sets the tone: 'Better a witty fool than a foolish wit'. This paradox establishes that in Illyria, the fool may be wiser than the supposedly wise.
findings.issue: The lesson presents 'Better a witty fool than a foolish wit' as Feste's own direct statement. In the text (Act 1, Scene 5), Feste attributes the line to a fictional authority he invents: 'For what says Quinapalus? Better a witty fool than a foolish wit'. Feste invokes the made-up sage 'Quinapalus' to give mock-authority to the aphorism. Presenting it as Feste's unattributed personal claim removes a layer of meta-comedy: the fool cites a non-existent philosopher, which is itself a joke. Students who attribute the line directly to Feste in the exam miss this layer of meaning.
findings.canonical_truth: Act 1, Scene 5: Feste says 'Those wits that think they have thee do very oft prove fools, and I that am sure I lack thee may pass for a wise man. For what says Quinapalus? Better a witty fool than a foolish wit.' Quinapalus is a name Feste invents; the aphorism is offered as if from a classical authority, which is part of the joke. The line is Feste's invention attributed to a fictional source, not a straightforward personal declaration.

findings.lesson_text: Olivia has locked herself away in mourning for her dead brother, vowing to reject all suitors for seven years.
findings.issue: The lesson says Olivia is mourning 'her dead brother' only. According to Act 1, Scene 2, the Captain tells Viola that Olivia's father also died shortly before her brother: 'A virtuous maid, the daughter of a count / That died some twelvemonth since … then leaving her / In the protection of his son, her brother, / Who shortly also died.' Olivia is mourning both her father and her brother. Valentine's report (Act 1.1) focuses on 'a brother's dead love' because that is the most recent loss, but the full picture includes both bereavements. Most lessons in this series follow the same simplification. Low severity because Valentine's report does centre the brother and the error is a common simplification in study materials.
findings.canonical_truth: Olivia's father (a count) died approximately a year before the play begins. Her brother died shortly after their father. She is mourning both. Valentine's Act 1.1 report focuses on the brother ('a brother's dead love, which she would keep fresh / And lasting in her sad remembrance'), and Olivia's own references in the play tend to emphasise the brother. The Captain's account in Act 1.2 confirms the father's death preceded the brother's.

findings.lesson_text: By becoming Cesario, she gains access to Orsino's court and a position of trust.
findings.issue: The lesson describes Viola's decision to disguise as 'a young man named Cesario', which is accurate in the play's narrative. However, Viola's original plan in Act 1, Scene 2 is to present herself as a eunuch — she says 'thou shalt present me as an eunuch to him' (referring to Orsino). The eunuch detail disappears quickly from the play and Shakespeare seems to abandon it, but the lesson omits this textual nuance entirely. For a close-reading exam context, students examining Act 1.2 closely may encounter the eunuch detail and should know it exists.
findings.canonical_truth: In Act 1, Scene 2, Viola tells the Captain: 'I'll serve this duke: / Thou shalt present me as an eunuch to him.' The word 'eunuch' implies a castrated male attendant, chosen to explain Viola's soft features and voice. This specific plan is never mentioned again and Viola enters Orsino's court simply as the young page Cesario. Commentators note that Shakespeare either changed his mind or the eunuch designation was dropped in performance. The lesson's description of Viola as simply disguising as 'a young man' is not wrong, but it omits the more precise textual evidence in the scene.

findings.lesson_text: Duke Orsino opens the play drowning in romantic melancholy: 'If music be the food of love, play on; / Give me excess of it'.
findings.issue: The lesson quotes Orsino as saying 'Give me excess of it' as the next line after 'play on', presenting a two-line version. The actual text continues: 'Give me excess of it, that, surfeiting, / The appetite may sicken and so die.' The lesson cuts the quote mid-clause, which changes the meaning: Orsino does not simply want more music — he wants so much that the appetite for love itself will die. Omitting 'that, surfeiting, / The appetite may sicken and so die' strips the self-destructive logic from the opening. This is a meaningful omission for AO2 analysis, though not an outright misquotation of the words presented.
findings.canonical_truth: Orsino's opening lines (Act 1, Scene 1): 'If music be the food of love, play on, / Give me excess of it; that surfeiting, / The appetite may sicken, and so die. / That strain again! it had a dying fall.' The purpose of wanting excess is to purge desire — the appetite sickening and dying. This self-defeating logic is central to Orsino's character and is lost by stopping at 'excess of it'.
